title: Medfly Gut Quiz
text:
Question 1: What are the 3 main components of the Medfly gut?


 A. Proximal, medial, and distal segments.  B. Anterior, middle, and posterior regions.  C. Foregut, midgut, hindgut.  D. Cranial, thoracic, and abdominal compartments. Submit





Question 2: Why would one choose to just sequence the gut and not the whole fly?


 A. Sequencing the gut is faster because gut DNA amplifies more efficiently than other tissues.   B. The gut contains higher concentrations of host DNA than the rest of the body.   C. The bacteria in the gut may be diluted out by the presence of bacteria from other tissues like reproductive organs.   D. Whole-fly sequencing prevents detection of microbial DNA entirely. 
Submit





Question 3: During tephritid metamorphosis, what happens to the larval gut?


 A. It enlarges and continues functioning in the adult.   B. It is partially retained and modified.   C. It is broken down and replaced with a newly formed adult gut.   D. It becomes the adult hindgut only.  Submit





Question 4: What are the 3 modes of microbial transmission?


 A. Vertical, horizontal, and environmental transmission.   B. Digestive, respiratory, and circulatory transmission.   C. Direct, indirect, and parasitic transmission.   D. Maternal, paternal, and sibling transmission.  Submit





Question 5: Why has horizontal/environmental transmission in Medfly not been directly proven?


 A. No bacteria have been detected in larvae.   B. The fruit environment is sterile.   C. Identical bacterial strains between hosts have not been demonstrated.   D. Sequencing methods are unavailable.  Submit

title: 1. Fruit Flies Quiz.
text:
Question 1: What is the more common family of fruit flies to the public?




















 A. Tephritidae   B. Drosophilidiae   C. Drosophilidae   D. Tephritidiae  Submit





Question 2: What commonly makes Tephritids “bad”?


 A. They have the highest fitness   B. Being colourful means they are better at being sneaky   C. The females use their ovipositor to lay their eggs in the fruit, where larvae develop   D. They’re bigger than Drosophilia, so they can do more  Submit





Question 3: What’s the other name for Tephritid flies?

Question 4: Why are Medflies the “more harsh” Tephritids?

title: 4. Microbial Analysis Quiz
text:
Question 1: What are the differences between alpha and beta diversity?


 A. Alpha diversity measures species richness across multiple ecosystems, while beta diversity measures genetic variation within a single species.   B. Alpha diversity measures total global biodiversity, while beta diversity measures local abundance.   C. Alpha diversity measures diversity within a single community, while beta diversity compares diversity between different communities.   D. Alpha diversity refers to microbial abundance, while beta diversity refers to microbial function. 

Submit






Question 2: What does Bray Curtis Disimilarity do?


 A. The phylogenetic distance between microbial species based on evolutionary history.   B. The richness of species within a single microbial community.   C. The compositional dissimilarity between two samples based on species abundance data.   D. The probability that two randomly selected individuals belong to the same species.  Submit





Question 3: I do some Bray Curtis disimilarity analysis based on fly lines from two different substrate samples in the lab, I get a value of 0.8, what does this mean?


 A. The two fly lines microbiotas are nearly identical in composition.   B. The two samples share exactly 80% of their microbial species.   C. The two samples are highly dissimilar in microbial community composition. 

Submit






Question 4: NMDS is an ordination technique, which is used to visualise similarities or dissimilarities in data. How does it do this?


 A. It does not preserve actual distances between samples, but instead maintains the rank order of those distances.   B. It projects samples onto axes that maximise total variance using eigenvectors from a covariance matrix.   C. It preserves exact pairwise distances by decomposing a distance matrix into principal coordinate axes.   D. It transforms abundance data into relative percentages and clusters samples based on shared taxa only.  Submit





Question 5: We learnt a bit about Bray Curtis dissimiliarity, how does this relate to NMDS?


 A. Bray–Curtis calculates phylogenetic relationships between microbes, which NMDS then uses to cluster samples.   B. NMDS requires Euclidean distances, so Bray–Curtis must first convert abundances into presence/absence.   C. Bray–Curtis measures compositional dissimilarity between samples, and NMDS uses these dissimilarities to visualise differences in low-dimensional space.   D. Bray–Curtis computes alpha diversity for each sample, which NMDS then projects onto axes to show individual sample diversity. 

Submit






Question 6: If we want to run NMDS in R, we use metaMDS(). What are the main components?


 A. k sets the number of random iterations, and distance chooses the method for standardizing alpha diversity.   B. k specifies the number of microbial taxa to include, and distance sets the physical distance between samples in the lab.   C. k sets the number of NMDS dimensions (axes), and distance specifies the dissimilarity metric used to calculate the distance matrix (e.g., "bray").   D. k defines the number of principal components, and distance calculates Euclidean distance for alpha diversity.  Submit

title: 2. Surface Sterilisation Quiz
text:
Question 1: What is surface sterilisation in this context?


 A. Washing the bench surface in the lab so you don’t contaminate the fly in microbiota experiments.   B. Washing the surface of the fly to remove external microbes   C. Putting fly in bath   D. Washing the outside of the cage which you will collect flies on, to not infect its mcirobiota  Submit






Question 2: What is a difference between bleach and ethanol?


 A.Ethanol destroys DNA, while bleach leaves DNA intact.   B. Bleach destroys DNA, while ethanol does not destroy DNA.  C.Both bleach and ethanol preserve DNA while killing microbes.   D. Bleach works only on bacteria, ethanol works only on viruses Submit







Question 3: How do we (in the Chapman group) give the Medfly a wash?


 A. Dunk it in ethanol for 1 minute, followed by 3x 30 seconds PBS washes.   B. Dunk it in ethanol for 30 seconds, followed by 3x 30 seconds PBS washes.  C. Dunk it in bleach for 1 minute, followed by 3x 30 seconds PBS washes   D. Dunk it in bleach for 30 seconds, followed by 3x 30 seconds PBS washes. Submit







Question 4: What might happen if we left the fly in the “sterilising” solution for too long?


 A. The fly might wake up and fly away.  B. The fly could become larger and easier to see.  C. The wings might change colour permanently.  D. The fly’s body could become damaged or too fragile to dissect properly. Submit







Question 5: Scenario: A Medfly has been taken straight from its cage, is then anesthesised and put in liquid nitrogen, and then the -80C. We take this fly from the -80m allow it to thaw, then put it in sterile PBS for 30 seconds, and repeat this 3x with 3 different sterile PBS washes. We then pick up the fly with sterile forceps and spread it on a sterile LB plate, we leave this plate to incubate. What is likely to grow?


 A. The plate is likely to grow bacteria but only because there’s bits of fly on it.   B. If the experiment works, then nothing as the fly has been washed.   C. The plate is likely to grow bacteria because the fly has not been washed.  Submit
